newsitem.title: USA: Powerful U.S. military rocket set for debut.
newsitem.headline: Powerful U.S. military rocket set for debut.

text.p: After a $1 billion development program, the most powerful unmanned rocket in the U.S. space fleet was ready on Saturday to make its debut, the U.S. Air Force said.
The Titan 4B was scheduled for blastoff from Cape Canaveral Air Station on Sunday between 12:36 and 4:46 p.m. EST (1736-2146 GMT).

The giant 20-storey rocket will carry a $200 million satellite capable of detecting enemy missile launches. Similar spacecraft provided an early warning of Iraqi Scud missile launches during the Gulf War.

The launch would be the culmination of 9-year, $1 billion program to improve the reliability and cargo capacity of the Titan 4 rocket, which has been the workhorse of the U.S. military space program since 1989.
The trade journal Aviation Week & Space Technology described the maiden flight as "one of the most important Air Force space missions ever conducted."

The Titan 4's solid rocket motors have been enlarged and manufactured with fewer joints from light-weight composite materials. Older metal-cased rockets were difficult to assemble and were blamed for a number of failures.

Other improvements included better steering, improved navigation and a new self-destruct system in case the rocket veers off course. The improvements are expected to reduce the time it takes to prepare the rocket for launch and boost its maximum cargo capacity to low earth orbit by 25 percent to 48,000 lbs.

The development of the new solid rockets was plagued with problems and ran five years behind schedule. A test motor exploded in September 1990, killing one worker, when a crane moving it collapsed. And another rocket exploded during a test firing in April 1991.

Aware of public concern in the Cape Canaveral area following the explosion last month of a much smaller Delta 2 rocket, the Air Force stressed in a news release that the Titan 4B was "a thoroughly tested and safe rocket."

Workers at NASA's nearby Kennedy Space Center were warned by announcements on Friday to take cover in air-conditioned shelters should there be an explosion within 20 seconds of launch. The rocket is laden with nearly half a million pounds of highly toxic rocket fuel.

The launch will be closely watched by NASA. The improved rocket is scheduled to blastoff in October with the space agency's Cassini probe to Saturn. The $3.4 billion spacecraft, the last of NASA's big-budget planetary explorers, is equipped with a radioactive power source.

Protesters have claimed that if the rocket carrying Cassini exploded it could scatter plutonium over a wide area and kill thousands of people. The space agency has denied there would be any release of radioactivity, even in a worse-case disaster.
